placementQuiz.q: A dynamic crosstab must enumerate column names at runtime. The safe pattern uses…
placementQuiz.explain: Build the pivot's column list from DISTINCT values and exec with format('%I') so identifiers are quoted-safe.

placementQuiz.q: On a moving-aggregate window function, which pair makes removals possible?
placementQuiz.explain: Inverse transition functions (MINVFUNC) let the aggregate subtract a value leaving the window — required for moving windows.

placementQuiz.q: `RANK(60000) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY salary DESC)` returns…
options: Where a salary of 60000 ranks among salaries as if inserted
placementQuiz.explain: WITHIN GROUP ordered-set aggregates compute the rank/position the argument would take inside the group.

options: Before the row's insert/update/delete on that relation
placementQuiz.explain: BEFORE runs before the operation on the target table; AFTER runs after it, with per-row or per-statement granularity.

placementQuiz.q: For a view you want updatable through a trigger. Which kind applies?
placementQuiz.explain: INSTEAD OF triggers on views intercept the write and run your procedure instead.

blocks.md: The fixed query hard-codes m1..m3; the function builds `col_list` from the months actually present, then interpolates it into the crosstab output declaration with `%s`. New months appear automatically without editing the report — that is the whole point of a dynamic pivot. When the category set is user-controlled, `%I` (identifier) quoting is what keeps a month name from becoming SQL structure.

**Identifier injection.** Never glue user-supplied category names into a pivot with plain `||`. `format('%I', name)` double-quotes and escapes the identifier; `%L` would quote a literal. A category value that becomes a column name is code, and must be quoted as such.

options: It quotes and escapes the identifier against injection
It only works in DO blocks
items.explain: %I quotes the identifier with double quotes and escapes embedded quotes, so a malicious product name cannot turn into SQL structure.

blocks.text: Rolling Analytics Metrics You Can Tune

blocks.label: custom window aggregate
blocks.code:
-- Custom moving-average aggregate: rolling analytics you can tune
CREATE FUNCTION mov_avg_sfunc(state internal, val numeric, window_start int, window_end int)
RETURNS internal LANGUAGE C AS '...';

CREATE FUNCTION mov_avg_final(state internal)
RETURNS numeric LANGUAGE C AS '...';

-- Moving window support for O(1) sliding
CREATE FUNCTION mov_avg_msfunc(state internal, val numeric, window_start int, window_end int)
RETURNS internal LANGUAGE C AS '...';

CREATE FUNCTION mov_avg_minvfunc(state internal, val numeric, window_start int, window_end int)
RETURNS internal LANGUAGE C AS '...';

CREATE AGGREGATE mov_avg(numeric) (
  SFUNC = mov_avg_sfunc,
  STYPE = internal,
  FINALFUNC = mov_avg_final,
  MSFUNC = mov_avg_msfunc,
  MINVFUNC = mov_avg_minvfunc,
  WINDOW = true
);

-- Usage: O(1) sliding average over a rolling 3-day window
SELECT emp_id,
       hire_date,
       salary,
       mov_avg(salary) OVER (ORDER BY hire_date
                             ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) AS rolling_avg
FROM employees;
blocks.pg: -- CREATE AGGREGATE ... WINDOW (PostgreSQL 14+); C implementation for the transition functions

blocks.md: Moving window support needs both msfunc and minvfunc: msfunc folds a new value in, minvfunc removes the value leaving the frame. Without minvfunc the server recomputes each window from scratch — O(k) per row instead of O(1). This is C-level machinery; PL/pgSQL cannot supply inverse transition functions.

The WindowAgg node sorts by the window ORDER BY, then slides the aggregate state across the frame. With msfunc/minvfunc the per-row transition cost is constant regardless of window width — the difference between a 3-day and a 90-day rolling metric collapses to zero. Tuning the aggregate (adding weights, decay, or session-aware state) is a matter of writing the transition functions, not the query.

items.q: Which transition pair lets a custom aggregate slide a window in constant time?
options: MSFUNC adds in / MINVFUNC subtracts out
items.explain: msfunc adds the new value, minvfunc removes the old one — O(1) per slide vs O(k) recompute.

items.q: Authoring a custom aggregate for a moving window means you must supply…
options: SFUNC/STYPE plus MSFUNC and inverse MINVFUNC
items.explain: Transition functions must be fast and IMMUTABLE; the msfunc/minvfunc pair lets the window slide incrementally.

blocks.text: RANK WITHIN GROUP and Gap Filling

blocks.label: hypothetical rank
blocks.code:
-- Where would a 100000 salary rank, as if inserted?
SELECT
  RANK(100000)       WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY salary) AS rank_of_100k,
  DENSE_RANK(100000) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY salary) AS dense_rank_of_100k,
  PERCENT_RANK(100000) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY salary) AS pct_rank_of_100k
FROM employees;
blocks.pg: -- Ordered-set aggregates: single pass, no temp row inserted
blocks.mysql: -- MySQL 8.0: no WITHIN GROUP for RANK; emulate with COUNT

blocks.label: ignore nulls gap fill
blocks.code:
SELECT day,
       sales,
       LAG(sales) IGNORE NULLS OVER (ORDER BY day) AS prev_reported,
       sales - LAG(sales) IGNORE NULLS OVER (ORDER BY day) AS delta_from_last_report
FROM daily_sales;
blocks.pg: -- LAG(... IGNORE NULLS) skips NULL rows while scanning back (PostgreSQL 15+)
blocks.mysql: -- MySQL: no IGNORE NULLS; emulate with a correlated last-non-null join

blocks.md: `LAG(sales) IGNORE NULLS` backfills a sparse series: it skips rows where the value is NULL and attaches the most recent non-NULL figure to the current row — the classic pattern for non-trading days, partial reporting, or telemetry gaps, without inventing data.

blocks.pg:

items.q: RANK(60000) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY salary DESC) returns…
options: The salary of the employee ranked 60000
Where a salary of 60000 would rank if inserted
items.explain: WITHIN GROUP asks: insert the argument — what is its rank in this distribution? Ordering follows the ORDER BY inside the call.

options: Backfilling sparse series with the last non-NULL value
items.explain: IGNORE NULLS skips NULL rows while scanning back, so the previous non-NULL figure attaches to the current row — gap fill, not speed.

blocks.md: **Triggers are invisible to EXPLAIN's node tree** — the plan shows the driving DML only. Use EXPLAIN ANALYZE's trailing `Triggers:` section to time them, and keep trigger bodies thin: they run inside the transaction and every row waits on them.

items.q: INSTEAD OF triggers can only be created on:
items.explain: INSTEAD OF is the view-writability mechanism; tables get BEFORE/AFTER row triggers.

items.q: RAISE EXCEPTION inside a BEFORE trigger:
options: Aborts the statement and rolls back the transaction
items.explain: An uncaught exception aborts the transaction — the standard way to enforce invariants beyond FK constraints.

revisionCard: Dynamic identifiers: EXECUTE format('%I', name) quotes identifiers — never bare || for pivot columns
Moving support: msfunc folds values in, minvfunc removes them — the O(1) sliding window pair
WITHIN GROUP: ordered-set aggregates rank the argument as if inserted (RANK/PERCENT_RANK)

glossary.def: Transition functions that add (msfunc) and remove (minvfunc) a value from a moving-aggregate window state.
A window aggregate whose state slides with the frame via inverse transition functions (O(1) per row).
A function answering 'where would this value rank?' without inserting any row.
An aggregate with a WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY ...) argument, e.g. RANK(x) WITHIN GROUP.
Clause supplying the ORDER BY and argument for ordered-set aggregates (RANK, percentiles).
A view-level trigger that intercepts a write and runs your procedure instead of the default action.
A crosstab whose category columns are built at runtime from the data, quoted with %I to stay safe.
